macroSectors.description: The macro-economic sector for businesses whose product is money itself: deposits, loans, insurance, investment management and the infrastructure of payments and markets. In India it links household savings with the borrowing needs of companies, individuals and government, and is shaped heavily by the RBI, SEBI and IRDAI. Its fortunes track the economic cycle, interest rates and capital market activity.

sectors.description: The single sector inside this macro group, covering banks, non-bank lenders, insurers, capital-market intermediaries and fintech companies. Together they collect savings, lend, carry risk and run the plumbing of payments and markets. They are judged with their own yardsticks - margins, asset quality, capital and assets under management - rather than ordinary operating margins.

industries.description: Non-bank lenders and finance-related companies: NBFCs, housing financiers, microfinance lenders, government-owned development financiers, investment and holding companies and other specialists.
industries.businessOverview: Most lenders here borrow wholesale - from banks, bond investors and sometimes the public - and lend on to individuals, small businesses or infrastructure projects at a higher rate. Each type has its own customer and risk profile: housing financiers lend long against property, microfinance lenders make small unsecured group loans, and development financiers fund state utilities and infrastructure. The industry also holds investment and holding companies, whose value comes from the shares and securities they own rather than from lending, plus niches such as asset reconstruction and securitisation. The RBI is the main regulator for almost all of them.
keyDemandDrivers: Credit demand from consumers, MSMEs and infrastructure
Cost and availability of bank and bond funding
Rural incomes and the property market
Government infrastructure and housing programmes
Equity market levels (for investment and holding companies)
keyRisks: Rising bad loans in a downturn
Competition from banks and fintech lenders

industries.description: Licensed banks that accept public deposits and lend: public sector, private sector and specialised (small finance and payments) banks.
industries.businessOverview: Banks gather deposits, keep part of them as mandatory cash and government bonds, and lend the rest to households, businesses and the government. Their profit is the spread between loan and deposit rates, plus fees, minus operating costs and provisions for bad loans. Public sector banks are majority-owned by the government, private banks by private shareholders, and differentiated banks serve niche customers under special licences. RBI monetary policy and supervision affect all of them at once.
keyDemandDrivers: Economic growth and loan demand
RBI policy rates and system liquidity
Household savings and deposit growth
Government spending and policy lending
Retail credit and digital banking adoption
keyRisks: Margin squeeze from rate cuts or costlier deposits

industries.description: Businesses that run, serve or sell through India's securities markets: asset managers, exchanges, depositories and registrars, brokers, distributors, rating agencies and capital-raising specialists.
industries.businessOverview: These firms earn fees linked to how much money is invested in markets and how actively it trades, rather than from lending. Market infrastructure (exchanges, depositories, registrars) has few competitors and strong network effects, while brokers, distributors and merchant bankers face more competition and swing more with sentiment. Asset managers and distributors earn a share of the assets they manage or influence, so both market levels and new inflows matter. SEBI regulates nearly all of them.
keyDemandDrivers: Shift of household savings into equities and mutual funds
Retail trading and derivatives activity
Equity market levels and volatility
IPO and bond issuance cycles
Growth in demat accounts and SIPs
keyRisks: Market downturns that cut volumes and AUM
SEBI changes to fees and products
Heavy reliance on derivatives trading income

industries.description: Companies that carry insurance risk (life, general and specialist insurers) and companies that sell or service insurance (brokers, aggregators, TPAs).
industries.businessOverview: Insurers collect premiums upfront, invest the money and pay claims or benefits later. Life insurers sell long-term protection, savings and pension policies and are judged on the value of new business they write. General insurers sell mostly one-year covers for health, motor, property and crops, earning from underwriting and from investing the premium float. Distributors and TPAs earn commissions and service fees without bearing claims risk, and IRDAI regulates products, solvency and expenses across the industry.
keyDemandDrivers: Low insurance penetration and rising incomes
Health-cost awareness and employer group cover
Vehicle sales and credit-linked covers
Bank and digital distribution reach
Interest rates and equity markets (investment income)
keyRisks: Rule changes on commissions, surrender values and pricing
Claim spikes from catastrophes or epidemics

industries.description: Technology-led companies that deliver financial services or the systems behind them, such as payments, digital lending platforms, financial marketplaces, card making and banking software.
industries.businessOverview: Fintech firms use software, data and mobile channels to offer payments, credit, insurance and investment products, often in partnership with banks, NBFCs and insurers that hold the licences and balance sheets. Revenue usually comes from small fees on large transaction volumes, commissions or software licences, so scale and pricing power decide profitability. India's public digital infrastructure - UPI, Aadhaar-based eKYC and account aggregators - lowers costs for everyone and keeps competition intense. RBI rules on payments and digital lending are the main regulatory factor.
keyDemandDrivers: Shift from cash to digital payments
Smartphone and internet adoption
Merchant digitisation
Demand for quick digital credit and insurance
Public digital infrastructure
keyRisks: Sudden RBI or payment-network rule changes
Dependence on bank and lender partners
Fraud, cyber attacks and data breaches
Losses and need for fresh funding

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Mostly government-owned lenders set up to finance national priorities such as power, railways, renewable energy, infrastructure, exports or small industry. They raise money mainly by selling bonds and lend large amounts for long periods.
productsAndServices: Long-term loans to state and central power utilities
Leasing of assets to government users
Refinance to banks and other lenders
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Wholesale financiers between the bond market (insurers, pension funds, banks, retail bondholders) and large public-sector or infrastructure borrowers. Several also act as nodal agencies that route government schemes in their sector.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn a thin but steady spread between lending rates and bond borrowing costs, made possible by strong credit ratings linked to government ownership. Some lease assets to government users on a cost-plus basis.
revenueSources: Interest on utility and project loans
Fees for scheme management and loan syndication
operatingCosts: Interest on bonds and bank borrowings
A small employee base (low operating costs)
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: State electricity distribution and generation companies, central PSUs, railways, renewable and infrastructure developers, and other lenders seeking refinance.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Lending follows government capex plans in power, transmission, railways and renewables, and the financial health of state utilities. Bond-market rates and investor appetite decide funding costs.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Lending is domestic; some raise foreign-currency loans or bonds and manage currency and rate risk with hedges.
basicIndustries.capexNote: They own few physical assets beyond leased ones; the balance sheet itself is the business.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Asset-liability management is central: very long loans are funded by bonds of mixed maturities, so refinancing and rate risk are watched closely.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI regulates them as infrastructure-finance NBFCs or all-India financial institutions, with exposure and provisioning norms; the government as owner sets mandates, dividends and board appointments.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Sovereign-linked ratings give low borrowing costs, and sector expertise plus policy roles are hard for private lenders to match.

drivers.impact: Central schemes for power, railways and green energy decide how much these lenders disburse.
Higher public capex means bigger loan books and more project pipelines.
Bond yields set their cost of funds and therefore their spread.
Rising power demand pushes utilities to borrow for generation, transmission and distribution.
Timely payments by state discoms keep asset quality healthy.

risks.detail: Heavy exposure to a few state utilities or government users magnifies any payment delay.
Changes in government priorities or scheme design can slow lending.
Margins narrow if borrowing costs rise faster than loans can be repriced.
Private infrastructure or renewable projects can turn into bad loans.
Government share sales add supply of shares in the market.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Lending is driven by multi-year government programmes rather than the consumer cycle, but asset quality depends on state finances and project execution.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Lenders that specialise in loans to buy, build or repair homes, plus loans against property. They are not banks, so they fund themselves by borrowing from banks and the bond market instead of from savings accounts.
productsAndServices: Home loans for salaried and self-employed borrowers
Affordable housing loans in smaller towns
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Downstream of the real estate market: they finance home buyers and developers, and are funded by banks, mutual funds, insurers, National Housing Bank refinance and depositors.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn the spread between home-loan rates and their borrowing cost over very long tenures, plus processing fees and gains from selling loan pools. Home loans are secured, so credit losses are usually low but spreads are thin.
revenueSources: Interest on home loans and LAP
Gains on assignment or securitisation of loans
operatingCosts: Sourcing payouts to loan agents and connectors
Legal and valuation checks on properties
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Individual home buyers, including low and middle-income families with informal incomes, and real estate developers needing project finance.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Housing demand, property prices, incomes and interest rates set loan demand, and government affordable-housing schemes add support. Banks offering cheaper home loans are the main competitive pressure.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Purely domestic lending; some raise funds through external commercial borrowings or foreign investors.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Spending goes mainly on branches and loan-origination technology.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Long loans funded by shorter borrowings create an asset-liability mismatch, so liquidity buffers and steady access to bonds and bank lines are critical.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI regulates HFCs, with the National Housing Bank handling supervision and refinance; rules cover capital, loan-to-value limits and deposits. RERA affects developer lending and tax benefits on home-loan interest support demand.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Low funding cost from a strong parent or rating, skill in assessing informal-income borrowers and branch reach in small towns.

drivers.impact: Lower rates cut funding costs and make EMIs affordable; rising rates do the opposite.
Home sales and prices drive loan demand and the safety of developer loans.
Affordable-housing subsidies and tax breaks on home loans widen the borrower base.
Bank appetite to lend to HFCs and to buy their loan pools sets funding availability.
Job security and income growth decide how many families buy homes.

risks.detail: Banks lure good borrowers away with cheaper balance-transfer offers.
A freeze in bond or bank funding can stall lending and raise costs.
Stalled projects make construction loans the riskiest part of the book.
Higher EMIs slow new demand and stretch weaker borrowers.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Retail home loans tend to be resilient, but growth and developer exposure follow the property cycle and interest rates.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies whose main business is holding and managing investments - shares, bonds, government securities or stakes in other businesses - rather than making products or giving retail loans. Their value largely tracks what they own.
productsAndServices: Portfolios of listed and unlisted shares
Government securities underwriting and dealing (primary dealers)
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Investors in the capital market rather than service providers: they deploy their own or group capital into securities and businesses. Primary dealers underwrite and trade government bonds at RBI auctions.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Through dividends, interest, trading gains and fair-value changes on holdings; primary dealers also earn underwriting commissions. Reported profit can jump around with market prices.
operatingCosts: Interest on borrowings for leveraged portfolios
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Few outside customers: the business is investing in companies and the bond market, and shareholders benefit through dividends and the value of holdings.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Earnings and book value follow equity prices, interest rates and the results of investee companies. For gilt dealers, the size of government borrowing and the direction of rates matter most.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Holdings are mainly Indian; global sentiment and foreign flows move the value of listed holdings.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Almost no physical assets; capital sits in securities.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Liquidity of holdings matters; gilt dealers run large bond books funded short-term, which are sensitive to rate moves.
basicIndustries.regulation: Most are RBI-registered NBFCs (investment and credit companies, core investment companies or primary dealers) with capital and leverage norms; SEBI listing rules apply.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Quality and liquidity of holdings, low leverage and a strong parent; for primary dealers, RBI authorisation and bond-market skill.

drivers.impact: Rising share prices lift portfolio values and trading gains.
Falling yields raise bond values; rising yields cause mark-to-market losses.
Dividends and value depend on how the companies held perform.
RBI rules on leverage and investments limit how the portfolio can be run.

risks.detail: A falling market cuts both profits and book value quickly.
Shares often trade well below the value of the investments held.
Bond-heavy books lose value when yields rise.
Loans or investments in group firms may not serve minority shareholders.
Many such shares trade thinly, so prices can be erratic.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Profits and net worth move with equity and bond markets.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Lending companies registered with the RBI that are not banks. They give loans for vehicles, gold, consumer goods, small businesses and personal needs, often to customers banks serve poorly, and fund themselves through borrowings.
productsAndServices: Vehicle loans (new and used cars, two-wheelers, trucks, tractors)
Co-branded credit cards and digital loans with partners
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream credit providers: they borrow wholesale from banks, mutual funds and bond investors (some also take public deposits) and lend retail, sourcing through dealers, retailers and fintech partners and often co-lending with banks.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Their loans carry higher rates than bank loans, so the spread over their higher borrowing cost is wider. Fees, insurance cross-sell and gains on selling loan pools add income, while credit losses are the main swing factor.
revenueSources: Gains on loan assignment and co-lending
operatingCosts: Sourcing commissions to dealers and partners
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Retail borrowers, self-employed people, small transport operators, farmers, small businesses and new-to-credit customers across urban and rural India.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Consumption, vehicle sales, rural incomes and MSME activity drive loan demand, while the cost and availability of bank and bond funding drive supply. Gold-loan demand also moves with gold prices.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic lending; some raise foreign-currency loans or bonds.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Branches and underwriting and collection technology need modest spending; capital is the real requirement for growth.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Borrowing tenures must match loan tenures; reliance on short-term commercial paper has caused liquidity crises before, so diversified funding matters.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI's scale-based regulation (base, middle, upper and top layers) sets capital, provisioning, governance and lending norms; RBI digital-lending and fair-practice rules and bank risk weights on loans to NBFCs also matter.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Niche underwriting skill, local collection teams, cheap funding from a strong parent or rating, and dealer and partner relationships.

drivers.impact: Strong demand for retail and MSME credit expands loan books.
Borrowing costs rise and fall faster than many fixed-rate loans reprice, moving margins.
Vehicle, durable and personal spending create loan demand.
Farm incomes drive tractor, two-wheeler and gold-loan demand and repayments.
RBI curbs on unsecured or digital lending can slow growth quickly.
Higher gold prices let gold lenders lend more against the same jewellery.

risks.detail: A loss of lender confidence can choke funding and force a growth slowdown.
Defaults rise quickly in unsecured and small-ticket loans during stress.
RBI can restrict products, pricing or sourcing practices.
Banks and fintech lenders compete for the best borrowers.
Dependence on one product or region magnifies local shocks.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Loan growth and credit losses follow consumption, vehicle sales and funding conditions.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: A catch-all for financial businesses that are neither banks nor regular lenders - for example asset reconstruction companies that buy bad loans, factoring and forex firms, gift-voucher platforms, advisory boutiques and app-based credit businesses.
productsAndServices: Purchase and recovery of stressed loans (asset reconstruction)
Gift cards, vouchers and rewards programmes
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Specialists at the edges of the lending system: asset reconstruction companies take bad loans off bank books, factors finance suppliers' invoices to large buyers, and voucher or rewards platforms serve corporates and banks.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: It depends on the model: asset reconstruction companies earn management fees plus a share of recoveries above the purchase price, factors and digital lenders earn interest spreads, and voucher, forex and advisory firms earn margins or fees.
revenueSources: Recoveries and management fees on stressed assets
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Banks and NBFCs selling bad loans, MSME suppliers, corporates running reward schemes, travellers and students needing forex, and retail app users.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Asset reconstruction depends on how many bad loans banks sell and how fast recoveries happen under IBC and SARFAESI; the other models follow consumer spending, trade flows and deal activity.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic; forex businesses depend on outbound travel and overseas education and are affected by rupee moves.
basicIndustries.capexNote: The needs are people, technology and capital to buy assets, not plants.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Asset reconstruction needs patient capital because recoveries take years; factors and short-term lenders turn money over quickly but rely on bank lines.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI regulates asset reconstruction companies under the SARFAESI Act, as well as factors, money changers and digital lending; the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code shapes recovery timelines; SEBI covers advisory and merchant banking.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Capital, recovery skill and bank relationships for reconstruction firms; partner networks and technology for platform models.

drivers.impact: RBI and insolvency rules decide how bad loans are sold, priced and resolved.
More stressed loans for sale means more buying opportunities for reconstruction firms.
Faster economic activity raises demand for invoice finance and small credit.
Spending on gifting, rewards and travel drives voucher and forex volumes.
Funding costs set margins for factoring and lending models.

risks.detail: Court and insolvency delays can erode the value of stressed assets bought.
RBI tightening on stressed-asset deals or digital credit can reshape the business.
Small-ticket digital and invoice loans can default in bulk.
Platform models often rely on a few banks or corporate clients.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Reconstruction firms find more assets in bad times, while consumer-linked models do better in good times.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that exist mainly to own large or controlling stakes in a business group's operating companies. They do little business of their own; their worth comes from those stakes.
productsAndServices: Some house financial-services subsidiaries (broking, lending, advisory)
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: At the top of a business group's ownership chain, between the promoter family and the operating companies.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Dividends from group companies, interest on loans to them, occasional brand fees and gains when stakes are sold. Consolidated results mirror the subsidiaries.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Their main counterparties are their own group companies; investors buy them as an indirect route into the group's businesses.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Value depends on the market price of the stakes held, the dividends paid and whether the gap to underlying value narrows or widens, for example on restructuring, mergers or buybacks.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Follows the businesses owned; some group companies operate globally.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Capital is tied up in shareholdings, not physical assets.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Minimal; cash flow is lumpy and depends on when group companies pay dividends.
basicIndustries.regulation: Those mainly holding group-company shares may need RBI registration as core investment companies with leverage limits; SEBI takeover and listing rules govern stake changes; dividend taxation affects how much value passes through.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: There is no operating moat of its own; quality of the underlying companies and promoter governance are what count.

drivers.impact: Prices of the listed stakes drive the value of the holding company.
Profits and dividends of investees flow up as income.
Mergers, demergers or simplification can narrow the holding discount.
Tax and RBI rules on core investment companies shape payouts and borrowing.

risks.detail: Shares often trade far below the value of the stakes held.
Thin trading makes prices volatile and exits hard.
Decisions may favour the promoter group over minority holders.
Value often rests on one or two group companies.
Dividends taxed at several layers reduce what reaches shareholders.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: It mirrors the industries of the companies held - steady if they are stable, cyclical if they are not.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Lenders that give small loans without collateral, mainly to women in low-income households, usually through groups that meet regularly and repay in small, frequent instalments.
productsAndServices: Small loans for home repair, sanitation or solar products
Small MSME loans for graduating borrowers
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Last-mile lenders funded by banks, development financiers and bond investors; field staff meet borrowers in their villages and neighbourhoods to disburse and collect.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Relatively high lending rates pay for a costly field-staff model and credit losses; profit is the spread left after these costs. Selling loan pools to banks, which count them as priority-sector loans, helps fund growth.
revenueSources: Gains on securitisation and assignment of loans
operatingCosts: Salaries of a large field staff
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Low-income women, rural households, small traders, artisans and farm-linked micro-businesses.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Credit demand from under-banked households is large; supply depends on bank funding and investor confidence. Several lenders chasing the same borrower is the main danger to the whole system.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic lending; foreign impact investors sometimes provide equity or debt.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Branches are small and simple; spending goes mainly on people and collection technology.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Short loan tenures with frequent repayments roughly match their borrowings, so collection efficiency directly drives liquidity.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI's microfinance framework defines microloans by household income, caps repayment burden relative to income and sets fair-practice rules; industry self-regulatory guardrails limit the number of lenders per borrower.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Dense field networks, borrower relationships, credit-bureau discipline and wide geographic spread; scale lowers funding cost.

drivers.impact: Village incomes drive both demand for loans and ability to repay.
A poor monsoon hurts farm-linked borrowers and collections.
Borrowers juggling several lenders push defaults up across the industry.
RBI and self-regulatory limits shape loan size, pricing and lender count per borrower.
Bank appetite to lend to MFIs or buy their pools governs growth.

risks.detail: Rapid industry growth can end in sharp spikes in defaults.
Floods, elections, unrest or local laws can halt collections in a region.
Loan-waiver talk or state action can make borrowers stop repaying.
Banks pull back from the segment during stress, raising costs.
Heavy exposure to a few states magnifies local shocks.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Credit costs jump during rural shocks or over-lending phases and then normalise.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Securitisation turns a pool of loans (vehicle, home, microfinance or other loans) into securities that investors can buy. Entities here are mostly special-purpose trusts or companies that hold such pools and pass the borrowers' repayments to investors.
productsAndServices: Pass-through certificates (PTCs) backed by loan pools
Senior and junior tranches with credit enhancement
Servicing and collection of pooled loans
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Sits between loan originators (banks, NBFCs, HFCs, MFIs) and investors (banks, mutual funds, insurers); rating agencies rate the tranches and trustees oversee the trust.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: The vehicle itself is built to pass cash through rather than earn a profit. The originator keeps any excess spread and servicing fees, investors earn the coupon, and arrangers and trustees earn fees.
revenueSources: Interest and principal from the loan pool (passed to investors)
Excess spread retained for the originator
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Banks buying retail or priority-sector pools, mutual funds, insurers and other fixed-income investors; originators use it to raise funds and free up capital.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Issuance rises when lenders need funding beyond bank loans or want to sell priority-sector pools; investor appetite depends on interest rates and how earlier pools performed.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: A domestic market; foreign portfolio investors take part occasionally.
basicIndustries.capexNote: These are legal structures with no physical assets.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Borrower collections are passed to investors on a fixed schedule; shortfalls hit the junior tranche and credit enhancement first.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI's securitisation directions set minimum holding periods, minimum retention by the originator and allowed structures; SEBI rules govern listed securitised debt; security receipts fall under the SARFAESI Act.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Originator quality, a clean pool-performance record and high ratings decide pricing; for equity investors this is rarely a listed operating business.

drivers.impact: Rate levels decide the yield investors demand and whether deals make sense for originators.
Fast retail lending creates more pools to sell.
RBI holding-period and retention rules shape deal volumes.
Defaults in underlying loans decide tranche losses and future appetite.

risks.detail: Borrower stress can exhaust credit enhancement and hit investors.
Early repayments shorten the life and yield of the securities.
New RBI or SEBI norms can make structures uneconomic.
Investors may struggle to sell before maturity.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Issuance and pool performance follow the credit cycle and funding conditions.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Banks in which the Government of India holds a majority stake. They take deposits from the public and lend to individuals, businesses, farmers and the government through large branch networks that reach small towns and villages.
productsAndServices: Insurance and mutual fund sales through branches
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Core of India's credit system: they collect household savings and channel them to companies, small businesses, farmers and the government (through bond holdings), and act as bankers to central and state governments.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Mainly the spread between interest earned on loans and bonds and interest paid on deposits. Fees and cross-selling add income, and treasury gains or losses on bonds can swing profits when rates move.
revenueSources: Interest on government and other bonds
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Retail savers across urban and rural India, large corporates and PSUs, MSMEs, farmers and government departments.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Loan demand follows economic activity, corporate investment and government infrastructure spending; deposit growth depends on household savings and competition from mutual funds and small-savings schemes. RBI rate changes reprice loans faster than deposits, moving margins.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic; some run overseas branches and GIFT City units serving Indian businesses and the diaspora. Global rates matter through bond yields.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Branches and core-banking IT are modest next to the balance sheet; growth instead consumes regulatory capital from retained profit, share sales or the government.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: The usual working-capital idea does not apply; what matters is liquidity (cash and bonds held under CRR, SLR and liquidity-coverage rules) and matching loan and deposit maturities.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI regulates them under the Banking Regulation Act (capital, CRR/SLR, priority-sector lending, NPA recognition, prompt corrective action); the government as owner appoints top management, injects capital and may steer policy lending.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: A huge low-cost deposit base, deep rural reach, government business and the trust that comes with state ownership; slower decisions and technology catch-up are common weaknesses.

drivers.impact: RBI rate moves change loan yields, deposit costs and the value of large bond holdings.
Corporate and infrastructure borrowing revive loan books in an upswing.
Recapitalisation, mergers, stake sales and directed lending shape returns.
Public capex creates demand for project and working-capital loans.
Recoveries lift profits; new stress forces heavy provisions.

risks.detail: Corporate or farm stress can raise NPAs and provisions quickly.
Policy lending, loan waivers or forced mergers can hurt minority shareholders.
Rising yields cause mark-to-market losses on big bond portfolios.
Savers moving to markets or private banks raise funding costs.
New share issues to fund growth or meet capital rules dilute holders.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Profits swing with the credit cycle - strong when bad loans recover, weak when they pile up.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Banks owned mainly by private shareholders - promoters, institutions and the public. They do the same basic job as public banks but usually lean more on retail customers, fee products and digital channels.
productsAndServices: Home, auto and personal loans and credit cards
Wealth management and third-party product sales
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Intermediaries between savers and borrowers, competing with public banks for deposits and with NBFCs and fintechs for retail and small-business loans; many own insurance, asset management and broking subsidiaries.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Net interest income is the main engine, backed by a large fee stream from cards, payments and sales of insurance and mutual funds. Higher-yield retail and unsecured loans lift margins but add credit risk.
revenueSources: Interest on retail and corporate loans
Insurance and mutual fund distribution commissions
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Urban and semi-urban retail customers, salaried professionals, SMEs and corporates; older regional private banks often have a loyal home-state base.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Retail credit demand, business working-capital needs and the ability to raise deposits drive growth. The fight for low-cost CASA deposits and RBI rules on unsecured lending set how fast they can grow.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Business is largely domestic, but foreign investors often own large stakes, so global fund flows affect valuations.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Spending goes on branches and technology; capital from profits and share issues is the real constraint on growth.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Judged through liquidity and the loan-to-deposit ratio rather than inventory; fast loan growth without matching deposits strains funding.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI licensing and supervision cover capital, CRR/SLR, priority-sector targets, promoter-holding limits and approval of top management; foreign-ownership limits are set by the government.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Strong brands, low-cost deposit franchises, technology, cross-selling and underwriting discipline protect the leaders; smaller banks rely on regional relationships.

drivers.impact: Retail and SME loan demand sets the pace of balance-sheet growth.
Rate cuts reprice floating-rate loans faster than deposits, squeezing margins for a while.
Spending on homes, cars and cards drives fee and loan growth.
The cost of attracting savings decides how cheaply they can fund loans.
Higher risk weights or curbs on certain loans can slow growth.
Digital channels cut costs but raise competition from fintechs.

risks.detail: Credit card and personal loan defaults can rise fast in a slowdown.
Slow deposit growth forces costlier funding or slower lending.
RBI scrutiny or management change can shake confidence.
Repeated outages can lead RBI to restrict new customers or products.
Smaller banks depend heavily on one or two states.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Loan growth and credit costs move with the economy, though strong franchises tend to stay profitable through it.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Banks with special, narrower licences - mainly small finance banks, which lend to small borrowers and the underbanked, and payments banks, which take small deposits and handle payments but cannot lend.
productsAndServices: Affordable home, vehicle and gold loans
Remittances, bill payments and cash withdrawal at agent points
Debit cards, wallets and UPI services
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: The last mile of the banking system, serving rural and semi-urban customers that larger banks find costly to reach. Many began as microfinance NBFCs and became banks to tap deposits.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Small finance banks earn wide spreads because their loans carry higher rates, offset by higher operating and credit costs. Payments banks earn transaction and remittance fees plus interest on the government securities where they must park deposits.
revenueSources: Commissions on insurance and other products
operatingCosts: Interest on deposits, often priced higher to attract savers
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Low-income households, women borrower groups, micro-entrepreneurs, small traders and farmers; payments banks also serve migrant workers and merchants.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand for small loans is large and under-served; growth depends on raising deposits cheaply and keeping collections steady. Rural incomes and competition from fintech lenders also matter.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Entirely domestic business.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Branch and agent expansion and core-banking systems need steady spending, but capital adequacy is the bigger constraint.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Liquidity and deposit stability matter most; reliance on bulk or high-cost deposits makes funding sensitive to confidence.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI's differentiated licences: small finance banks must meet priority-sector and small-loan requirements, payments banks cannot lend and have caps on balances per customer, and moving to a universal licence needs RBI approval.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Deep local knowledge, field collection processes and low-cost reach to remote areas; building a trusted deposit franchise is the main barrier.

drivers.impact: Rural incomes decide loan demand and repayment capacity.
Farm stress quickly shows up in small-loan collections.
Deposit rates they must offer set the cost of funding.
Licence conditions limit products and decide when they can graduate to full banks.
Formal credit reaching new borrowers expands their market.

risks.detail: Over-indebted borrowers or local disruptions can spike defaults.
Smaller brands must pay more for deposits than large banks.
Many depend on a few states.
RBI restrictions can halt new accounts or products.
Apps compete for payments and small-ticket credit.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Asset quality is sensitive to rural incomes, local events and borrower over-borrowing.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that run mutual funds and other investment pools for investors. They pool money from many people, invest it in shares, bonds or other assets, and charge a fee based on the money they manage.
productsAndServices: Equity, debt and hybrid mutual funds
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: They manufacture investment products; distributors, banks, brokers and online platforms sell them, while registrars, custodians and depositories handle records and safekeeping.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: A management fee charged as a share of assets under management, within SEBI's limits on scheme expense ratios. Equity funds earn higher fees than debt or index funds, so the product mix matters as much as total AUM.
revenueSources: Management fees on mutual fund AUM
PMS and AIF fees, including performance fees
operatingCosts: Employee costs for fund managers and sales
Distributor commissions not borne by schemes
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Retail investors (often via SIPs), wealthy individuals, corporates, banks, insurers and retirement funds.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Inflows depend on households shifting savings from deposits and gold to market products, SIP habits, fund returns and distributor reach. Market levels change AUM even without new money.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly Indian investors and assets; some manage offshore funds or advise global investors on Indian equities.
basicIndustries.capexNote: A people-and-technology business with little physical capital.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Fees are taken from scheme assets on a running basis, so receivables are low and cash generation is strong.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI mutual fund rules govern expense-ratio caps, scheme categories, skin-in-the-game requirements and disclosures; AMFI sets distributor norms; changes in tax on fund gains affect demand.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Brand, long performance records, distribution reach and scale (low cost per rupee managed); the move to passive funds pressures fees.

drivers.impact: Rising markets lift AUM and attract fresh equity inflows.
Savings moving from deposits and gold into funds widens the base.
Changes to expense-ratio caps or commissions reset fee yields.
Rate moves shift money between debt funds, deposits and equities.
Changes in tax on fund gains alter the appeal of debt and equity schemes.

risks.detail: Falling prices shrink AUM and can trigger redemptions.
Lower allowed expense ratios reduce revenue per rupee managed.
Lagging returns push investors to rival fund houses.
Growth of low-fee index funds compresses margins.
Exit of star fund managers can cause outflows.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: AUM and fees follow markets, but recurring SIP flows and sticky assets soften the swings.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: The back-office plumbing of the market: depositories hold shares and bonds in electronic (demat) form, and registrars keep investor records for mutual funds and companies. They earn small fees on a very large number of accounts and transactions.
productsAndServices: Demat holding and transfer of securities
Mutual fund registrar and transfer agency
Share registry and IPO processing for companies
Investor statements, data and technology services
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Market infrastructure used by exchanges, brokers, depository participants, fund houses and listed companies; they serve the whole market rather than competing for end investors.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Depositories charge annual fees to issuers, charges on debit transactions and fees for KYC, e-voting and data; registrars charge fund houses fees linked to assets or folios. Costs are largely fixed, so higher volumes lift margins.
revenueSources: Registrar fees from mutual funds and companies
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Listed and unlisted companies, mutual funds, depository participants (brokers and banks), exchanges and, indirectly, every investor.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Growth in demat accounts, trading activity, new listings and mutual fund folios drives revenue, while SEBI pricing decisions can reset fee levels.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic; some sell software or services abroad and in GIFT City.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Resilient systems, data centres and security need continuous investment.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Light; most fees are collected in advance or quickly.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI recognises depositories and clearing corporations as market infrastructure institutions and registers registrars and KRAs, controlling ownership, governance and fees.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Regulatory licences, network effects, high switching costs for fund houses and issuers, and very few competitors.

drivers.impact: More trading, IPOs and new investors raise transaction and account fees.
Rising fund AUM and folios lift registrar income.
SEBI decisions on fees and processes directly change revenue.
New digital services (KYC, data, e-voting) add income but need investment.

risks.detail: SEBI can lower or restructure charges paid by investors and issuers.
Fewer transactions and listings reduce variable income.
Failures invite penalties and reputational damage.
Registrars depend on a limited number of large fund houses.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Annual and record-keeping fees are steady, while transaction and IPO income follows market activity.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Firms that sell and advise on investment products made by others - mainly mutual funds, plus insurance, bonds, PMS and AIFs. Wealth managers in this group look after the money of affluent families.
productsAndServices: Bonds, structured products and fixed deposits
Online platforms for sub-distributors and advisers
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Downstream of fund houses and insurers, linking product makers to investors through relationship managers, partner networks or digital platforms.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Mostly trail commissions paid by fund houses as a share of client assets, so income grows with the assets they influence; wealth managers also earn on structured products and advisory fees.
revenueSources: Trail commissions on mutual fund assets
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Retail investors in smaller towns reached through partner networks, affluent and high-net-worth families, and independent advisers using their platforms.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Market levels, SIP flows and the shift of savings to market products drive assets; investors moving to direct plans or fee-only advisers shrink the commission pool.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic; some also serve non-resident Indians.
basicIndustries.capexNote: A people-driven business with light technology spend.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Light; commissions arrive regularly from product makers.
basicIndustries.regulation: AMFI registration and SEBI rules on distributors, separation of advice from distribution, commission disclosure and expense-ratio limits; IRDAI governs insurance commissions.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Sticky client relationships, trust, adviser networks and broad product shelves; low-cost platforms compete on price.

drivers.impact: Rising markets increase client assets and trail income.
More families investing in funds enlarges the client base.
Rules on commissions and advice can change how they are paid.
Direct and app-based investing competes with commission-based distribution.

risks.detail: Lower expense ratios flow through to lower trail payouts.
Investors bypassing distributors shrink the paying base.
Asset-linked income falls with prices.
Relationship managers leaving can take clients with them.
Unsuitable product sales invite penalties and reputational harm.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Income tracks market values and investor sentiment.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Credit rating agencies give opinions, as letter grades, on how likely a borrower is to repay its debt. Companies and lenders pay for ratings because banks, regulators and bond investors rely on them.
productsAndServices: Ratings on bonds, debentures and commercial paper
Ratings for SMEs, infrastructure and municipal bonds
Research, industry reports and risk analytics
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Information intermediaries between borrowers (companies, NBFCs, municipalities) and lenders or investors; their grades decide bank capital needs and whether investors may buy a paper.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Mostly an issuer-pays model: an initial fee when a debt is rated and annual surveillance fees while it is outstanding. Research, analytics and outsourcing services add non-rating income.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Corporates, banks, NBFCs, infrastructure projects and municipal bodies, plus investors and lenders who buy research.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Bond and commercial-paper issuance, bank credit growth and securitisation volumes drive new mandates, while surveillance fees on existing ratings give a recurring base.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Ratings are domestic; some have analytics or research arms serving global clients.
basicIndustries.capexNote: An analyst-driven service business.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Fees are collected upfront or yearly, so receivables are modest.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI's credit rating agency regulations cover conflicts of interest, disclosures and rating performance; RBI accreditation lets bank-loan ratings be used for capital calculations.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Reputation, regulatory accreditation and long rating histories make entry hard; the industry has few players.

drivers.impact: Busy bond and commercial-paper markets mean more instruments to rate.
Bank lending to rated borrowers drives bank-loan rating demand.
Lower rates encourage companies to issue more bonds.
Rules requiring rated instruments create steady demand.

risks.detail: Fewer bonds and loans mean fewer new mandates.
Missing a major default damages credibility.
SEBI can fine or restrict agencies over lapses.
Agencies may undercut each other to win issuers.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Surveillance fees are steady, while new rating income follows borrowing and bond-market activity.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Exchanges are organised marketplaces where buyers and sellers trade shares, derivatives, commodities or electricity under set rules. They earn a small fee on each trade and charge for listings, data and technology access.
productsAndServices: Listing services for companies and bonds
Market data feeds and index licensing
Clearing and settlement through clearing corporations
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Core market infrastructure: brokers bring orders, the exchange matches them, clearing corporations settle them and depositories record ownership; data goes to brokers, vendors and fund managers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Transaction charges on traded value or option premium, plus listing fees, data and index licence fees, co-location charges and income on clearing funds. Costs are largely fixed, so higher volumes bring strong operating leverage.
operatingCosts: Investor protection and other mandated funds
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Brokers and their clients (retail, institutional, proprietary traders), listed companies, power producers and distributors for power exchanges, and data users.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Volatility, retail participation, derivatives activity, IPO pipelines and gaps in power supply drive volumes; curbs on speculative trading can reduce them.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic markets, with some international activity through GIFT City; global events drive volatility and volumes.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Trading systems, data centres and cybersecurity need constant upgrades.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Light; fees are collected promptly, and member margins held for settlement are client money, not the exchange's own working capital.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI recognises and regulates stock and commodity exchanges, approving products and fees, capping ownership and setting guarantee-fund rules; power exchanges come under CERC, including any market-coupling decisions.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Liquidity attracts more liquidity: network effects, licences and ownership caps make new entry very difficult.

drivers.impact: More traders and higher volatility raise transaction volumes.
SEBI or CERC changes to products, fees or trading rules move volumes directly.
Faster, reliable systems and new products are needed to keep volumes.
Supply shortages and price swings drive spot power trading.
New listings add listing fees and investor interest.

risks.detail: Rules to cool retail F&O trading can cut the largest revenue stream.
Regulators or competition can force lower transaction charges.
Glitches bring penalties and loss of trust.
Pooling of power-exchange bids could weaken a leading exchange's edge.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Volumes jump in active markets and fade in quiet ones, but dominant exchanges stay profitable.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Brokers let investors buy and sell shares, derivatives and commodities on exchanges, and often add margin funding, research, wealth management and investment banking. They range from low-cost app-based brokers to full-service and wealth firms.
productsAndServices: Equity, derivatives, currency and commodity broking
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: The front end of the market: they bring retail and institutional orders to exchanges and route settlement through clearing corporations and depositories.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Brokerage per order or as a share of trade value, interest on margin funding and on funds kept with exchanges, depository charges and distribution commissions; wealth firms earn fees on assets they manage or advise.
operatingCosts: Interest on borrowings for margin funding
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Retail traders and investors, wealthy families, institutions such as mutual funds and foreign investors, and companies raising capital.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: New investor accounts, retail derivatives trading, market sentiment and IPO activity drive revenue; competition and SEBI rules shape what brokers can charge.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic; institutional brokers depend partly on foreign investor flows.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Spending goes on trading apps and technology rather than physical assets.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Client margins and settlement need large funds and bank guarantees, and margin-funding books are financed with borrowings, making part of the business lender-like.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI stock-broker rules govern client-fund handling, margins, the derivatives framework, charge disclosure and cybersecurity; exchange-level fee rules affect broker economics.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Scale, brand and app experience for discount brokers; client relationships and research for full-service and wealth firms.

drivers.impact: Bull markets bring new accounts and higher trading volumes.
SEBI changes to derivatives, margins or client funds directly hit revenue.
Low-cost apps have reshaped pricing and customer acquisition.
Rates set the yield on margin funding and the cost of borrowing for it.
Volatile phases raise derivatives activity.

risks.detail: Restrictions on retail derivatives can sharply cut order volumes.
Activity and new accounts drop in prolonged downturns.
Zero or flat-fee brokerage compresses revenue per trade.
App outages on busy days cause losses and complaints.
Sharp market moves can leave margin-funded clients unable to pay.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Revenue rises sharply in bull markets and shrinks when trading activity dries up.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Smaller specialists that help companies raise money or support market activity - merchant bankers and IPO lead managers (especially for SME IPOs), market makers, corporate advisers, debenture trustees and similar firms.
productsAndServices: SME IPO lead management and market making
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Service providers to issuers and exchanges at the capital-raising end of the market, working alongside brokers, registrars, rating agencies and lawyers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Issue-management fees (often a share of money raised), market-making spreads, advisory retainers and success fees; some also keep stakes in companies they bring to market.
operatingCosts: Capital tied up in underwriting and market making
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Small and mid-sized companies raising capital, their promoters, investors and bond issuers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Business follows the IPO and fundraising cycle, especially on SME platforms; tighter SME listing norms reduce deal flow.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Domestic.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Advisory work needs little fixed capital.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Market making and underwriting tie up money in share inventory; fee receipts are lumpy and deal-based.
basicIndustries.regulation: SEBI merchant banker, debenture trustee and research analyst regulations, plus SME listing rules and exchange due-diligence requirements.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Relationships, deal track record and SEBI registration; low entry barriers mean many small players.

drivers.impact: Hot primary markets bring a flood of mandates.
The number of SME and mainboard issues sets fee income.
SEBI tightening on SME IPOs or merchant bankers can cut deal flow.

risks.detail: Fee income can vanish in a weak market.
SEBI scrutiny of SME issues can bring penalties or bans.
Poor post-listing performance of their IPOs hurts future mandates.
Shares held for market making can fall in value.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Fee income booms in hot primary markets and dries up in downturns.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Insurers that cover non-life risks - motor, health, property, crops, travel and business liabilities - usually with one-year policies. They collect premiums upfront, pay claims when losses happen and invest the money in between.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Risk carriers between customers (individuals, businesses, government schemes) and reinsurers; they sell through agents, brokers, banks, motor dealers and online aggregators.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Underwriting profit (earned premium minus claims and expenses) plus investment income on the float of premiums held before claims are paid. Many run close to break-even on underwriting and earn mainly from investments.
revenueSources: Commission on business ceded to reinsurers
operatingCosts: Commissions to agents, brokers and banks
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Vehicle owners, families and employers buying health cover, businesses insuring assets and liabilities, and farmers through government crop schemes.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Vehicle sales, rising medical costs and awareness, credit-linked covers, economic activity and government schemes drive premiums; competition and pricing freedom set margins.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Risks are mainly Indian, but reinsurance links them to global reinsurers; reinsurers also write overseas business, so global catastrophe losses and pricing matter.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Branches and technology; capital is held mainly to meet solvency rules.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Premiums arrive before claims, creating a float; long-tail motor third-party and liability claims can take years to settle, so reserving discipline matters.
basicIndustries.regulation: IRDAI regulates product filing, solvency, expense limits, claims practices and investments; motor third-party premiums are set by the authorities rather than by insurers; GST applies to premiums.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Pricing discipline, efficient claims handling, distribution tie-ups with banks and dealers, hospital networks and data-driven underwriting.

drivers.impact: Rising medical costs and awareness push health insurance demand.
New vehicle sales drive motor premiums.
IRDAI rules on pricing, expenses and products shape margins.
Bond yields decide investment income on the float.
Floods, cyclones and other disasters drive spikes in claims.
Equity gains boost investment income in good markets.

risks.detail: A large disaster can wipe out a year's underwriting profit.
Hospital and repair costs can rise faster than premiums.
Aggressive pricing in group health and motor erodes margins.
Underestimated long-tail claims hit future profits.
Third-party motor rates may not keep up with claims.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Demand for cover is steady, but profits swing with claims experience, catastrophes and investment gains.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Insurers that pay out on death or provide long-term savings and pensions. Customers pay premiums for many years, and the insurer invests that money and pays benefits as the policy promises.
productsAndServices: Non-participating savings plans with guaranteed returns
Group fund management for gratuity and superannuation
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Long-term savings managers and risk carriers; they sell mainly through bank partners (bancassurance), agents, brokers and online channels, and invest heavily in government bonds and equities.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Profit is earned over each policy's life from mortality margins (protection), investment spreads (savings and annuities) and fund charges (ULIPs). Accounting profit lags sales, so value of new business and embedded value are the main yardsticks.
revenueSources: Single premiums from annuities and group business
operatingCosts: Benefits paid and reserves set aside
Commissions to banks, agents and brokers
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Salaried and self-employed families, retirees, borrowers needing loan cover and employers buying group schemes.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Rising incomes, a large protection gap, retirement needs, bank-partner reach, tax incentives and equity markets (for ULIPs) drive demand; interest rates affect guaranteed-product pricing and annuity appeal.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Business is domestic; foreign partners are common shareholders within government ownership limits, and global reinsurers take part of the mortality risk.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Distribution and technology rather than physical assets; capital is held for solvency.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Premiums arrive long before benefits are paid, building a large investment book; matching assets to guaranteed liabilities is critical.
basicIndustries.regulation: IRDAI regulates products, surrender values, commissions and expenses, solvency and investments; tax rules on premiums and maturity proceeds influence demand; GST applies to premiums.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Access to distribution (especially bank tie-ups), brand trust, high persistency, product design and cost efficiency.

drivers.impact: Rates shape pricing of guaranteed plans, annuity demand and investment returns.
Strong equity markets lift ULIP sales and fund-based income.
IRDAI rules on surrender values and commissions change product margins.
Changes in tax benefits on premiums or maturity alter savings-product appeal.
Income growth and protection awareness drive term and savings sales.

risks.detail: New surrender-value or commission rules can cut new-business margins.
Withdrawal of tax benefits can hurt high-premium savings sales.
Falling rates make guaranteed promises costly if not hedged.
Losing or sharing a bank channel can hit sales sharply.
Poor persistency erodes profitability and invites regulatory action.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Protection and renewal premiums are steady, while ULIP sales and investment values follow equity markets.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: A small, residual bucket for insurance businesses that do not fit neatly into life or general insurance - for example specialist credit or export-credit covers, micro-insurance or holding structures that own insurers.
productsAndServices: Trade credit, surety and export-credit covers
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Niche risk carriers or owners of insurers, working with banks, exporters, government schemes and reinsurers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Like other insurers, through underwriting margins and investment income on premiums held; holding structures earn dividends and value from the insurers they own.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Exporters, lenders, MSMEs, farmers in government schemes and low-income households.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Trade volumes, credit growth, government scheme design and awareness drive premiums; claims depend on default cycles and weather.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Export-credit and trade covers are tied to overseas buyer risk, and reinsurance links them to global markets.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Capital is held for solvency rather than physical assets.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Premium float as for other insurers; claims on credit-type covers can bunch together in downturns.
basicIndustries.regulation: IRDAI licensing, product approval and solvency rules; government-owned specialist insurers also follow ministry mandates.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Specialist underwriting data, government backing or mandates and reinsurer relationships.

drivers.impact: IRDAI product and solvency rules decide what niche covers can be offered.
Scheme design and subsidies drive crop and export-credit volumes.
Trade activity and buyer defaults abroad move credit-cover premiums and claims.
More lending to small firms raises demand for credit guarantees.

risks.detail: Credit and weather covers can see many claims at once.
Changes to government schemes can shrink the business.
Global reinsurance price rises squeeze margins.
Few comparable listed companies make valuation hard.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Premiums are fairly steady, but credit-type and weather-linked claims rise in bad years.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Businesses that sell or service insurance without carrying the risk themselves - insurance brokers, corporate agents, online insurance marketplaces and third-party administrators (TPAs) that process health claims for insurers and employers.
productsAndServices: Insurance broking for retail and corporate clients
Health claims processing and cashless hospital settlement (TPA)
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Between insurers and policyholders: they source policies and service claims, and TPAs connect insurers, hospitals and insured employees or families.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Commissions and brokerage as a share of premium sold, within IRDAI's overall expense limits for insurers, plus administration fees per policy or member for TPAs and fees for marketing or technology services.
revenueSources: Marketing and rewards fees from insurers
operatingCosts: Medical review staff and hospital network management (TPAs)
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Insurers, which pay commissions and fees; corporates buying group health and employee benefits; retail buyers; and hospitals in TPA networks.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Insurance penetration, employer group health cover, medical inflation and digital adoption drive volumes; insurers handling claims in-house and expense rules shape margins.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mainly domestic; some brokers and TPAs serve overseas insurers or clients.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Technology platforms and service centres need modest spending.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Light; commissions and fees come from insurers on regular cycles, though some dues from insurers or government schemes can stretch.
basicIndustries.regulation: IRDAI regulates brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators and TPAs, and its limits on insurers' expenses cap what can be paid to distributors; health-claims rules shape TPA work.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Scale in claims processing, hospital network relationships, insurer tie-ups, brand and low customer acquisition cost.

drivers.impact: More health cover and higher claims volumes raise TPA and broking income.
IRDAI expense and distribution rules decide commission levels.
Online buying and digital claims shift share to tech-led players.
More first-time buyers enlarge the market for distributors.

risks.detail: Insurers or regulators can cut payouts to intermediaries.
Insurers handling claims or sales themselves reduce TPA and broker roles.
A few large insurers or corporates may dominate revenue.
Health and personal data breaches bring legal and reputational damage.
A regulator-backed common insurance marketplace could reduce the role of private aggregators.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Insurance renewals and group health cover stay fairly steady through economic cycles.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Technology companies that provide financial services or the systems behind them - digital payments, online lending and insurance marketplaces, payment card making, banking software and identity checks. Many earn small fees on very large volumes.
productsAndServices: Digital lending platforms with partner banks and NBFCs
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: The technology layer between banks, NBFCs and insurers and their customers or merchants; they run on bank partners, card networks and UPI rails and sell to merchants, consumers and financial institutions.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Fees on payments processed, commissions from lenders and insurers for customers sourced, software subscriptions or licences, sale of cards and devices, and interest where they lend. Scale lowers cost per transaction, so profits hinge on volume and pricing power.
revenueSources: Interest income on loans or float
operatingCosts: Credit losses where they share loan risk
Chips and materials for card makers
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Merchants, consumers, banks, NBFCs, insurers and government agencies.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: The shift from cash to digital payments, smartphone use, merchant digitisation and credit demand drive volumes; pricing is shaped by rules such as zero merchant fees on UPI.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic; some sell software, card or identity solutions abroad and handle cross-border payments.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Platforms need ongoing software and data-centre spending, and card or device makers need machinery.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Payment firms hold settlement money that belongs to merchants; card makers carry chip inventory and bank receivables; lending models tie up capital in loans.
basicIndustries.regulation: RBI rules on payment aggregators, prepaid instruments, digital lending and default-loss guarantees, NPCI rules for UPI, IRDAI and SEBI rules for marketplaces, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Network effects, merchant and bank relationships, licences, brand and data; low switching costs in payments keep pricing competitive.

drivers.impact: New payment rails and mobile adoption expand what can be done digitally.
RBI and NPCI rules decide pricing, licences and lending models.
Online spending and digital habits drive transaction volumes.
Demand for digital loans raises distribution and lending income.
Support for digital payments and public digital infrastructure lowers costs and widens reach.

risks.detail: Sudden licensing, pricing or lending rules can upend business models.
Zero-fee payment rails leave little room for profit.
Loss of a bank or lender partner can halt products.
Breaches cause losses, penalties and loss of trust.
Loss-making firms depend on fresh funding to keep growing.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Payment volumes grow steadily, while lending and marketplace income follow the credit cycle.
